investigations__LUNG FUNCTION__Spirometr.front: Which single spirometry value distinguishes an obstructive from a restrictive pattern?
investigations__LUNG FUNCTION__Spirometr.back: The FEV₁/FVC ratio. A reduced ratio (< 0.70 or below the LLN) defines obstruction; a preserved or raised ratio with a low FVC suggests restriction.

investigations__LUNG FUNCTION__Spirometr.front: Define the spirometric obstructive pattern and give two causes.
investigations__LUNG FUNCTION__Spirometr.back: Reduced FEV₁ with FEV₁/FVC < 0.70 (or below LLN). Causes: COPD and asthma.

investigations__LUNG FUNCTION__Spirometr.front: What confirms a restrictive defect, and why can't spirometry do it alone?
investigations__LUNG FUNCTION__Spirometr.back: A reduced total lung capacity (TLC) on lung volume measurement (plethysmography or gas dilution). Spirometry only shows a low FVC with a preserved ratio, which is suggestive but not confirmatory, because gas trapping in obstruction can also lower FVC.

investigations__LUNG FUNCTION__Spirometr.front: What defines significant bronchodilator reversibility, and what does it favour?
investigations__LUNG FUNCTION__Spirometr.back: An increase in FEV₁ of ≥ 12% AND ≥ 200 mL after a bronchodilator. It favours asthma over COPD.

investigations__LUNG FUNCTION__Spirometr.front: What are the ATS/ERS acceptability and repeatability requirements for spirometry?
investigations__LUNG FUNCTION__Spirometr.back: At least 3 acceptable blows (good start, no cough in the first second, exhalation ≥ 6 s to a plateau), with the best two FEV₁ and best two FVC values agreeing within 150 mL.

investigations__LUNG FUNCTION__Spirometr.front: What four variables do GLI-2012 predicted spirometry values depend on?
investigations__LUNG FUNCTION__Spirometr.back: Age, height, sex and ethnicity. Height is the strongest determinant of lung volume; age causes decline after the early-20s plateau; males have larger lungs for a given height; and ethnicity-specific coefficients (Caucasian, African-American, NE Asian, SE Asian, other/mixed) correct for differences in body build.

investigations__LUNG FUNCTION__Spirometr.front: How is the lower limit of normal (LLN) defined, and what z-score corresponds to it?
investigations__LUNG FUNCTION__Spirometr.back: The LLN is the 5th centile of the healthy reference distribution, meaning only 5% of genuinely healthy people fall below it. It corresponds to a z-score of -1.64. Values below this are considered abnormal for that individual.

investigations__LUNG FUNCTION__Spirometr.front: Why does the fixed FEV1/FVC ratio of 0.70 over-diagnose obstruction in the elderly and under-diagnose it in the young?
investigations__LUNG FUNCTION__Spirometr.back: The FEV1/FVC ratio physiologically declines with age. A fixed 0.70 line sits below the true LLN in older people (so normal ageing lungs are wrongly called obstructed = over-diagnosis) and above the LLN in young adults (so early obstruction is missed = under-diagnosis). The GLI LLN adjusts for age and avoids both errors.

investigations__LUNG FUNCTION__Spirometr.front: What advantage does a z-score have over percent-predicted for interpreting spirometry?
investigations__LUNG FUNCTION__Spirometr.back: A z-score expresses the result as the number of standard deviations from the predicted mean and accounts for the fact that the spread of normal values changes with age and height. This makes the abnormal threshold constant (z < -1.64) at all ages, whereas a fixed '80% of predicted' rule does not correctly track the normal range across the lifespan.

investigations__LUNG FUNCTION__Spirometr.front: State the GOLD severity grades of airflow obstruction by FEV1 % predicted.
investigations__LUNG FUNCTION__Spirometr.back: GOLD 1 (mild): FEV1 >=80% predicted; GOLD 2 (moderate): 50-79%; GOLD 3 (severe): 30-49%; GOLD 4 (very severe): <30% predicted. Severity is graded only after obstruction is confirmed.

investigations__LUNG FUNCTION__Spirometr.front: What is the purpose of bronchodilator reversibility testing?
investigations__LUNG FUNCTION__Spirometr.back: To measure the change in airflow (FEV₁/FVC) after a short-acting bronchodilator, demonstrating a reversible airflow component. It supports a diagnosis of asthma and helps distinguish asthma (reversible) from COPD (largely fixed obstruction).

investigations__LUNG FUNCTION__Spirometr.front: Describe the standard protocol for a bronchodilator reversibility test.
investigations__LUNG FUNCTION__Spirometr.back: Record baseline spirometry, give a short-acting bronchodilator (commonly 400 mcg inhaled salbutamol via spacer), then repeat spirometry at 15-20 minutes. Prior bronchodilators should be withheld so the baseline is not already dilated.

investigations__LUNG FUNCTION__Spirometr.front: What are the significant reversibility thresholds?
investigations__LUNG FUNCTION__Spirometr.back: ATS/ERS 2022: a change of >10% of the predicted value for FEV₁ or FVC. Older widely quoted criterion: an FEV₁ improvement of ≥12% AND ≥200 mL.

investigations__LUNG FUNCTION__Spirometr.front: How do asthma and COPD typically differ on reversibility testing?
investigations__LUNG FUNCTION__Spirometr.back: Asthma shows marked reversibility and obstruction may normalise (a large response ≥400 mL strongly favours asthma). COPD shows minimal change with persistent obstruction after the bronchodilator.

investigations__LUNG FUNCTION__Spirometr.front: Does a negative reversibility test exclude asthma?
investigations__LUNG FUNCTION__Spirometr.back: No. Asthmatic airflow limitation is variable and may be near-normal at the time of testing, so a negative test does not exclude asthma. Pursue further objective tests such as a peak-flow diary, FeNO, or bronchial challenge.

investigations__LUNG FUNCTION__Spirometr.front: On a standard flow-volume loop, which limb is plotted upward and what are the two axes?
investigations__LUNG FUNCTION__Spirometr.back: Flow (L/s) is the y-axis and volume (L) is the x-axis. By convention expiratory flow is plotted upward (above the volume axis) and inspiratory flow downward, forming a closed loop from a forced expiration then forced inspiration.

investigations__LUNG FUNCTION__Spirometr.front: What flow-volume loop shape suggests diffuse intrathoracic airflow obstruction (asthma/COPD)?
investigations__LUNG FUNCTION__Spirometr.back: A concave, scooped-out expiratory limb with a reduced peak expiratory flow. Volumes may be preserved or hyperinflated, but expiratory flow falls disproportionately at low lung volumes.

investigations__LUNG FUNCTION__Spirometr.front: A plateau confined to the INSPIRATORY limb indicates what type of large-airway obstruction, and give an example.
investigations__LUNG FUNCTION__Spirometr.back: Variable extrathoracic obstruction. During inspiration negative intraluminal pressure collapses the extrathoracic airway. Examples: vocal cord dysfunction, extrathoracic tracheomalacia.

investigations__LUNG FUNCTION__Spirometr.front: A box-like loop with plateaus on BOTH the inspiratory and expiratory limbs signifies what, with examples.
investigations__LUNG FUNCTION__Spirometr.back: Fixed large-airway obstruction: a rigid lesion that cannot change calibre with pressure. Examples: tracheal stenosis, large retrosternal goitre, glottic/tracheal tumour.

investigations__LUNG FUNCTION__Spirometr.front: How does a restrictive flow-volume loop differ from an obstructive one?
investigations__LUNG FUNCTION__Spirometr.back: Restriction gives a tall, narrow 'witch's hat' loop shifted toward low volume: reduced lung volumes with a preserved (steep, convex) expiratory contour. Obstruction gives a normal/large volume loop with a scooped concave expiratory limb.

investigations__LUNG FUNCTION__Spirometr.front: What does peak expiratory flow (PEF) physiologically measure?
investigations__LUNG FUNCTION__Spirometr.back: The maximum flow rate during a forced expiration from full inflation, reflecting effort-dependent flow through the LARGE airways. It is measured in L/min and is technique-dependent.

investigations__LUNG FUNCTION__Spirometr.front: How is a PEF reading correctly performed?
investigations__LUNG FUNCTION__Spirometr.back: Stand/sit upright, reset the pointer to zero, take a maximal deep breath in, seal lips around the mouthpiece, and give a short, hard, fast blast. Record the BEST OF 3 attempts.

investigations__LUNG FUNCTION__Spirometr.front: How is diurnal PEF variability calculated and what threshold supports asthma?
investigations__LUNG FUNCTION__Spirometr.back: (Highest − Lowest) ÷ Highest × 100. Variability >20% on ≥3 days per week over 2 weeks supports variable airflow obstruction and a diagnosis of asthma. PEF is typically lowest on waking (morning dipping).

investigations__LUNG FUNCTION__Spirometr.front: How does serial PEF help diagnose occupational asthma?
investigations__LUNG FUNCTION__Spirometr.back: The patient keeps a diary of PEF across work days and rest days. A consistent fall in PEF during work periods with recovery away from work implicates a workplace sensitiser and warrants referral.

investigations__LUNG FUNCTION__Spirometr.front: State the acute asthma severity thresholds based on PEF (% best/predicted).
investigations__LUNG FUNCTION__Spirometr.back: Moderate: PEF ≥50–75%. Acute severe: PEF 33–50%. Life-threatening: PEF <33%. Below 50% requires urgent treatment; below 33% is a medical emergency.

investigations__LUNG FUNCTION__Provocati.front: What does bronchial provocation testing measure, and when is it indicated?
investigations__LUNG FUNCTION__Provocati.back: It measures airway hyper-responsiveness. It is indicated when asthma is suspected clinically but spirometry is normal/non-diagnostic and there is no bronchodilator reversibility.

The provocative concentration (PC20) or dose (PD20) of methacholine that causes a 20% fall in FEV₁ from baseline, interpolated from the dose–response curve. A lower value means greater hyper-responsiveness.

investigations__LUNG FUNCTION__Provocati.front: How does methacholine act, and how is it classed compared with mannitol/exercise?
investigations__LUNG FUNCTION__Provocati.back: Methacholine is a direct challenge agent, acting on muscarinic M₃ receptors on airway smooth muscle. Mannitol, exercise and hypertonic saline are indirect agents that work via inflammatory mediator release.

investigations__LUNG FUNCTION__Provocati.front: Why is a negative methacholine challenge clinically valuable?
investigations__LUNG FUNCTION__Provocati.back: Because of its very high negative predictive value, a negative test largely excludes current asthma in a symptomatic patient.

investigations__LUNG FUNCTION__Provocati.front: List key contraindications to methacholine challenge.
investigations__LUNG FUNCTION__Provocati.back: Severe airflow limitation (FEV₁ <50% predicted or <1 L), recent MI or stroke, known aortic/cerebral aneurysm, uncontrolled hypertension; relative: pregnancy/breastfeeding, moderate airflow limitation, current respiratory infection.

investigations__LUNG FUNCTION__Provocati.front: What is the key mechanistic difference between direct (methacholine) and indirect (mannitol/exercise) bronchial provocation tests?
investigations__LUNG FUNCTION__Provocati.back: Direct agents act straight on airway smooth-muscle receptors (sensitive, non-specific). Indirect stimuli dehydrate/osmotically load the airway surface, triggering endogenous mediator release from inflamed mast cells/eosinophils, so they reflect airway inflammation and are more specific for asthma/EIB.

investigations__LUNG FUNCTION__Provocati.front: What FEV₁ fall defines a positive exercise challenge for exercise-induced bronchoconstriction (EIB)?
investigations__LUNG FUNCTION__Provocati.back: A ≥10% fall in FEV₁ from baseline after exercise. For eucapnic voluntary hyperpnoea (EVH) a ≥15% fall is often used to increase specificity.

investigations__LUNG FUNCTION__Provocati.front: What defines a positive mannitol challenge?
investigations__LUNG FUNCTION__Provocati.back: A ≥15% fall in FEV₁ from baseline, OR a ≥10% incremental fall between two consecutive doses. A lower PD₁₅ (provoking dose) indicates greater airway hyper-responsiveness.

investigations__LUNG FUNCTION__Provocati.front: Why does a positive indirect provocation test have therapeutic value beyond diagnosis?
investigations__LUNG FUNCTION__Provocati.back: Because indirect tests reflect active airway inflammation, a positive result predicts a good response to inhaled corticosteroids, guiding treatment as well as confirming EIB/airway hyper-responsiveness.

investigations__LUNG FUNCTION__Provocati.front: What are key safety prerequisites before performing a bronchial provocation challenge?
investigations__LUNG FUNCTION__Provocati.back: Adequate stable baseline FEV₁ (usually ≥70% predicted), withholding of bronchodilators/caffeine, and immediate availability of a bronchodilator, oxygen, and resuscitation equipment. Testing at low lung function risks severe bronchospasm.

investigations__LUNG FUNCTION__Provocati.front: What does a raised FeNO indicate?
investigations__LUNG FUNCTION__Provocati.back: Eosinophilic (type-2 / T2-high) airway inflammation. IL-13 upregulates inducible nitric oxide synthase (iNOS) in bronchial epithelium, increasing exhaled NO.

investigations__LUNG FUNCTION__Provocati.front: What is the standard FeNO measurement and its units?
investigations__LUNG FUNCTION__Provocati.back: A single-breath online test at a constant exhalation flow of 50 mL/s, reported as FeNO50 in parts per billion (ppb).

investigations__LUNG FUNCTION__Provocati.front: What are the NICE positive FeNO thresholds for adults and children?
investigations__LUNG FUNCTION__Provocati.back: Adults: FeNO ≥ 40 ppb is positive. Children (5–16 years): FeNO ≥ 35 ppb is positive. Both support an asthma diagnosis.
Smoking, inhaled or oral corticosteroids, and recent forced expiratory manoeuvres/exercise. These can give a falsely reassuring normal result.

investigations__LUNG FUNCTION__Provocati.front: What are the clinical uses of FeNO in asthma?
investigations__LUNG FUNCTION__Provocati.back: Supporting the diagnosis, predicting inhaled corticosteroid responsiveness, and monitoring treatment adherence (a high FeNO despite ICS suggests poor adherence or technique).

investigations__LUNG FUNCTION__Gas Trans.front: What does transfer factor (TLCO/DLCO) actually measure?
investigations__LUNG FUNCTION__Gas Trans.back: The diffusing capacity of the lung for carbon monoxide — how efficiently gas crosses the alveolar-capillary membrane. A single breath of low-concentration CO is used because CO binds haemoglobin ~250× more avidly than O₂, making uptake diffusion-limited and dependent on surface area, membrane thickness and capillary haemoglobin.

investigations__LUNG FUNCTION__Gas Trans.front: What is KCO and how does it differ from TLCO?
investigations__LUNG FUNCTION__Gas Trans.back: KCO is the transfer coefficient = TLCO corrected for (divided by) the alveolar volume Vₐ actually reached. TLCO is a whole-lung value; KCO is transfer factor per litre of ventilated lung, used to separate loss of lung tissue from restriction that only reduces lung size.

investigations__LUNG FUNCTION__Gas Trans.front: Give four causes of a LOW TLCO.
investigations__LUNG FUNCTION__Gas Trans.back: Emphysema (destroyed alveolar surface), pulmonary fibrosis/ILD (thickened membrane), pulmonary vascular disease such as PE or pulmonary hypertension, and anaemia (less haemoglobin to bind CO). Emphysema and fibrosis lower both TLCO and KCO.

investigations__LUNG FUNCTION__Gas Trans.front: Give four causes of a RAISED TLCO.
investigations__LUNG FUNCTION__Gas Trans.back: Pulmonary (alveolar) haemorrhage — extravasated red cells bind CO within alveoli; polycythaemia; asthma; and left-to-right cardiac shunt (increased pulmonary blood volume).

investigations__LUNG FUNCTION__Gas Trans.front: How does haemoglobin affect TLCO and how is it handled?
investigations__LUNG FUNCTION__Gas Trans.back: CO uptake depends on capillary haemoglobin, so TLCO must be corrected for measured Hb. Uncorrected, anaemia falsely lowers TLCO and polycythaemia falsely raises it, mimicking or masking membrane disease.

investigations__LUNG FUNCTION__Gas Trans.front: Which lung volumes cannot be measured by simple spirometry, and why?
investigations__LUNG FUNCTION__Gas Trans.back: RV, FRC and TLC cannot be measured because they all include the residual volume — the gas remaining after maximal expiration, which is never breathed out at the mouth. Spirometry only captures actively moved air (VC, FEV1 and their subdivisions), so absolute volumes need plethysmography or gas dilution.

investigations__LUNG FUNCTION__Gas Trans.front: How does body plethysmography measure thoracic gas volume?
investigations__LUNG FUNCTION__Gas Trans.back: The patient pants against a closed shutter inside a sealed rigid box; chest movements compress and decompress the trapped gas, and reciprocal changes in box and mouth pressure are applied to Boyle's law (P1V1 = P2V2) to derive thoracic gas volume at FRC. It measures ALL compressible intrathoracic gas, including gas behind closed airways and in bullae.

investigations__LUNG FUNCTION__Gas Trans.front: Why do helium dilution and nitrogen washout underestimate lung volumes in severe COPD/bullae?
investigations__LUNG FUNCTION__Gas Trans.back: Both methods only sample gas that communicates with open airways — helium equilibrates only into ventilated spaces and washout only collects nitrogen from communicating regions. Non-communicating trapped gas (bullae, severely obstructed units) is missed, so RV, FRC and TLC are underestimated. Plethysmography reads higher and is the gold standard.

investigations__LUNG FUNCTION__Gas Trans.front: What lung-volume pattern defines a restrictive defect versus hyperinflation?
investigations__LUNG FUNCTION__Gas Trans.back: Restriction is defined by a low TLC (below the lower limit of normal, roughly <80% predicted). Hyperinflation with gas trapping shows a raised TLC, raised RV and an increased RV/TLC ratio, typical of COPD/emphysema.

investigations__LUNG FUNCTION__Gas Trans.front: How are RV and TLC derived once FRC is measured by a gas-dilution method?
investigations__LUNG FUNCTION__Gas Trans.back: FRC is measured directly; then RV = FRC minus ERV, and TLC = RV + VC (slow vital capacity from spirometry). So gas dilution and washout give FRC first and the other static volumes are calculated from it.

investigations__LUNG FUNCTION__Gas Trans.front: What does body plethysmography measure to derive airway resistance?
investigations__LUNG FUNCTION__Gas Trans.back: It measures alveolar pressure (via a mouth shutter during panting) and airflow to give Raw, plus thoracic gas volume (Boyle's law) so resistance can be normalised to lung volume as sGaw.

investigations__LUNG FUNCTION__Gas Trans.front: Define specific airway conductance (sGaw).
investigations__LUNG FUNCTION__Gas Trans.back: sGaw = Gaw / lung volume, where Gaw (conductance) = 1/Raw. It corrects conductance for the lung volume at which it was measured, giving a volume-independent index of airway calibre.

investigations__LUNG FUNCTION__Gas Trans.front: How do Raw and sGaw change in airflow obstruction?
investigations__LUNG FUNCTION__Gas Trans.back: Raw is raised (airways narrowed, more driving pressure needed) and sGaw is low. A significant rise in sGaw (~30-40%) after a bronchodilator indicates reversibility, supporting asthma.

investigations__LUNG FUNCTION__Gas Trans.front: Why is airway resistance testing useful when spirometry fails?
investigations__LUNG FUNCTION__Gas Trans.back: It is effort-independent, needing only quiet tidal panting rather than a forced maximal blow, so it stays valid in young children, frail patients, or those who cannot coordinate spirometry.

investigations__LUNG FUNCTION__Gas Trans.front: Why must Raw always be reported with lung volume?
investigations__LUNG FUNCTION__Gas Trans.back: Resistance falls as the lungs inflate because airways are tethered open at higher volumes; without the corresponding volume Raw cannot be interpreted, which is why sGaw (volume-corrected) is preferred.

investigations__LUNG FUNCTION__Gas Trans.front: What does the Lung Clearance Index (LCI) measure?
investigations__LUNG FUNCTION__Gas Trans.back: Ventilation inhomogeneity / small-airways disease. It quantifies how evenly inhaled gas is distributed throughout the lungs, derived from a multiple-breath inert-gas washout during tidal breathing.

investigations__LUNG FUNCTION__Gas Trans.front: State the formula for LCI.
investigations__LUNG FUNCTION__Gas Trans.back: LCI = Cumulative Expired Volume (CEV) ÷ Functional Residual Capacity (FRC). It is the number of lung-volume turnovers needed to clear the tracer gas down to 1/40th (2.5%) of its starting concentration.

investigations__LUNG FUNCTION__Gas Trans.front: To what fraction of starting concentration is the tracer gas washed out in MBW?
investigations__LUNG FUNCTION__Gas Trans.back: To 1/40th, i.e. 2.5%, of the initial end-tidal tracer concentration. The cumulative expired volume required to reach this endpoint forms the numerator of the LCI.

investigations__LUNG FUNCTION__Gas Trans.front: Why is LCI preferred over spirometry in early cystic fibrosis?
investigations__LUNG FUNCTION__Gas Trans.back: It is more sensitive and detects small-airways disease earlier; LCI can be abnormal while FEV1 is still normal. It is also effort-independent and feasible in young children as it uses tidal breathing.

investigations__LUNG FUNCTION__Gas Trans.front: Which tracer gases are used in multiple-breath washout, and how is LCI value affected by disease?
investigations__LUNG FUNCTION__Gas Trans.back: Resident nitrogen (washed out with 100% oxygen) or exogenous SF6 (washed in then out). A higher LCI indicates worse ventilation distribution / more inhomogeneity.

investigations__LUNG FUNCTION__Spirometr.question: A 68-year-old smoker has post-bronchodilator spirometry showing FEV₁ 55% predicted and FEV₁/FVC 0.58. Which pattern does this represent?
options: Obstructive pattern
Restrictive pattern
Mixed pattern with reduced TLC
Normal spirometry
Isolated reduced gas transfer
investigations__LUNG FUNCTION__Spirometr.explanation: An FEV₁/FVC ratio below 0.70 with a reduced FEV₁ defines an obstructive defect. In a long-term smoker this pattern is consistent with COPD.

investigations__LUNG FUNCTION__Spirometr.question: Which spirometry result best suggests a restrictive process?
options: Reduced FEV₁ with FEV₁/FVC 0.55
Reduced FVC with FEV₁/FVC 0.85
Normal FVC with FEV₁/FVC 0.60
Raised FVC with reduced FEV₁
Reduced FEV₁ with normal FVC and low ratio
investigations__LUNG FUNCTION__Spirometr.explanation: Restriction produces a reduced FVC with a preserved or raised FEV₁/FVC ratio because both volumes fall proportionately. This pattern should be confirmed by a reduced TLC on lung volume testing.

investigations__LUNG FUNCTION__Spirometr.question: What is the accepted threshold change in FEV₁ that indicates significant bronchodilator reversibility?
options: ≥ 5% and ≥ 100 mL
≥ 12% only, with no volume criterion
Any fall in FEV₁/FVC ratio below 0.70
investigations__LUNG FUNCTION__Spirometr.explanation: Significant reversibility is an increase in FEV₁ of at least 12% and at least 200 mL after a bronchodilator. This finding supports a diagnosis of asthma rather than COPD.

investigations__LUNG FUNCTION__Spirometr.question: A patient's spirometry report gives an FEV1/FVC z-score of -1.90. How should this be interpreted?
options: Within the normal range
Below the lower limit of normal, indicating airflow obstruction
Above the upper limit of normal
Consistent with a restrictive defect
Uninterpretable without the percent-predicted value
investigations__LUNG FUNCTION__Spirometr.answer: Below the lower limit of normal, indicating airflow obstruction
investigations__LUNG FUNCTION__Spirometr.explanation: The LLN corresponds to a z-score of -1.64, so a value of -1.90 lies below the 5th centile. A reduced FEV1/FVC below the LLN defines airflow obstruction. The z-score alone is sufficient because it is already age, height and sex independent.

investigations__LUNG FUNCTION__Spirometr.question: Why does applying a fixed FEV1/FVC cut-off of 0.70 tend to over-diagnose airflow obstruction in elderly patients?
options: Elderly patients cannot perform a valid forced expiration
The FEV1/FVC ratio physiologically declines with age, so a fixed line falls below the true LLN in older people
Height decreases with age, artificially raising the ratio
GLI equations are not validated above age 80
Bronchodilators lose efficacy with age
investigations__LUNG FUNCTION__Spirometr.answer: The FEV1/FVC ratio physiologically declines with age, so a fixed line falls below the true LLN in older people
investigations__LUNG FUNCTION__Spirometr.explanation: The FEV1/FVC ratio normally falls as lungs age, so in older people the true LLN drops below 0.70. A rigid 0.70 threshold therefore labels many healthy ageing lungs as obstructed. Interpreting against the age-adjusted GLI LLN corrects this over-diagnosis.

investigations__LUNG FUNCTION__Spirometr.question: A patient with confirmed airflow obstruction has an FEV1 of 42% predicted. Which GOLD severity grade does this represent?
options: Mild (GOLD 1)
Moderate (GOLD 2)
Severe (GOLD 3)
Very severe (GOLD 4)
Normal
investigations__LUNG FUNCTION__Spirometr.explanation: An FEV1 of 30-49% predicted defines severe obstruction, GOLD grade 3. A value of 42% falls squarely within this band. Grades 1, 2 and 4 correspond to >=80%, 50-79% and <30% respectively.

investigations__LUNG FUNCTION__Spirometr.question: A patient has obstructive spirometry. After 400 mcg salbutamol, FEV₁ rises from 2.00 L to 2.40 L (predicted FEV₁ 3.00 L). Which statement best describes this result?
options: It is significant reversibility, meeting both the ≥12% and ≥200 mL criteria
It is non-significant because FVC did not change
It is non-significant because the rise is under 200 mL
It cannot be interpreted without a bronchial challenge test
It confirms COPD because obstruction was present at baseline
investigations__LUNG FUNCTION__Spirometr.answer: It is significant reversibility, meeting both the ≥12% and ≥200 mL criteria
investigations__LUNG FUNCTION__Spirometr.explanation: The FEV₁ rise is 400 mL, which is 20% of the baseline of 2.00 L. This exceeds both the ≥12% and the ≥200 mL thresholds and represents significant reversibility, strongly favouring asthma.

investigations__LUNG FUNCTION__Spirometr.question: Which agent and repeat-timing combination is standard for bronchodilator reversibility testing?
options: 400 mcg salbutamol, repeat spirometry at 15-20 minutes
Oral prednisolone, repeat spirometry at 24 hours
Long-acting beta-agonist, repeat spirometry at 5 minutes
Nebulised saline, repeat spirometry at 60 minutes
Intravenous aminophylline, repeat spirometry immediately
investigations__LUNG FUNCTION__Spirometr.answer: 400 mcg salbutamol, repeat spirometry at 15-20 minutes
investigations__LUNG FUNCTION__Spirometr.explanation: A short-acting beta-agonist such as 400 mcg inhaled salbutamol is given and spirometry is repeated at 15-20 minutes. This interval allows the drug to reach peak bronchodilator effect before reassessment.

investigations__LUNG FUNCTION__Spirometr.question: A patient with suspected asthma has a negative bronchodilator reversibility test. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Pursue further objective testing such as peak-flow variability or FeNO
Confidently exclude asthma and stop the workup
Diagnose COPD regardless of smoking history
Immediately start long-term oral corticosteroids
Repeat the test after giving intravenous fluids
investigations__LUNG FUNCTION__Spirometr.answer: Pursue further objective testing such as peak-flow variability or FeNO
investigations__LUNG FUNCTION__Spirometr.explanation: Asthmatic airflow limitation is variable, so a single negative reversibility test does not exclude asthma. Additional objective evidence such as peak-flow variability, FeNO, or a bronchial challenge should be sought before the diagnosis is discarded.

investigations__LUNG FUNCTION__Spirometr.question: A 54-year-old with progressive stridor has a flow-volume loop showing a plateau of the expiratory limb only, with a normal-shaped inspiratory limb. Where is the lesion?
options: Variable intrathoracic large airway
Variable extrathoracic large airway
Fixed upper airway lesion
Diffuse small airways disease
Restrictive parenchymal disease
investigations__LUNG FUNCTION__Spirometr.explanation: During forced expiration positive pleural pressure compresses intrathoracic airways, limiting flow and producing an expiratory plateau. Because inspiration splints these airways open, the inspiratory limb is preserved. This isolated expiratory plateau localises the variable lesion within the thorax.

investigations__LUNG FUNCTION__Spirometr.question: Which flow-volume loop appearance is most characteristic of a large fixed upper-airway obstruction such as tracheal stenosis?
options: Scooped concave expiratory limb with normal inspiration
Plateau of both inspiratory and expiratory limbs giving a box-like loop
Tall narrow loop shifted to low volume
Inspiratory plateau with normal expiratory limb
Normal loop with an exaggerated peak expiratory flow
investigations__LUNG FUNCTION__Spirometr.answer: Plateau of both inspiratory and expiratory limbs giving a box-like loop
investigations__LUNG FUNCTION__Spirometr.explanation: A fixed lesion has a rigid calibre that cannot vary with the changing transmural pressures of inspiration and expiration. Flow is therefore capped in both directions, flattening both limbs into a box shape. This dual plateau is the classic signature of fixed obstruction.

investigations__LUNG FUNCTION__Spirometr.question: A young woman with episodic breathlessness labelled 'refractory asthma' has a flow-volume loop with a flattened inspiratory limb. What is the single most important immediate interpretation?
options: The finding confirms severe small-airways asthma
It indicates a restrictive ventilatory defect
It points to a large-airway (extrathoracic) obstruction that must not be missed
It is a normal variant of forced inspiration
It reflects reversible bronchoconstriction responsive to salbutamol
investigations__LUNG FUNCTION__Spirometr.answer: It points to a large-airway (extrathoracic) obstruction that must not be missed
investigations__LUNG FUNCTION__Spirometr.explanation: Flattening of the inspiratory limb signals variable extrathoracic large-airway obstruction such as vocal cord dysfunction or a laryngeal lesion, which is frequently mislabelled as asthma. Recognising the plateau redirects investigation toward direct airway visualisation and prevents dangerous mismanagement.

investigations__LUNG FUNCTION__Spirometr.question: A 24-year-old with suspected asthma keeps a 2-week PEF diary. His highest reading is 500 L/min and his lowest is 380 L/min on a typical day. What is his diurnal variability, and does it support asthma?
options: 24% — supports asthma
24% — argues against asthma
32% — supports asthma
12% — supports asthma
12% — argues against asthma
investigations__LUNG FUNCTION__Spirometr.explanation: Variability is (500 − 380) ÷ 500 × 100 = 24%. A value greater than 20% on repeated days indicates variable airflow obstruction and supports a diagnosis of asthma.

investigations__LUNG FUNCTION__Spirometr.question: A patient in the emergency department with acute asthma has a PEF of 30% of her personal best, along with a silent chest and SpO₂ of 90%. How should this attack be classified?
options: Moderate acute asthma
Acute severe asthma
Life-threatening asthma
Near-fatal asthma requiring only observation
Well-controlled chronic asthma
investigations__LUNG FUNCTION__Spirometr.explanation: A PEF below 33% of best or predicted defines life-threatening asthma, and a silent chest with SpO₂ under 92% confirms this category. It mandates immediate senior support, oxygen, nebulised bronchodilators and critical care review.

investigations__LUNG FUNCTION__Spirometr.question: Which feature of a serial PEF record most specifically points towards occupational asthma?
options: A PEF that is consistently lowest on waking every morning
A fall in PEF during work days with recovery on days off
A single PEF reading below 80% of predicted
PEF that rises by 15% after inhaled bronchodilator
PEF that is identical at every time point through the day
investigations__LUNG FUNCTION__Spirometr.answer: A fall in PEF during work days with recovery on days off
investigations__LUNG FUNCTION__Spirometr.explanation: Occupational asthma is identified when serial PEF falls during work periods and recovers away from work, linking symptoms to a workplace sensitiser. This work-versus-rest pattern is the hallmark that distinguishes it from non-occupational asthma.

investigations__LUNG FUNCTION__Provocati.question: A 26-year-old with intermittent cough and wheeze has normal spirometry and no bronchodilator reversibility. Which parameter defines a positive methacholine challenge?
options: A 12% and 200 mL rise in FEV₁ after methacholine
A 20% fall in FEV₁ from baseline
A 15% rise in peak expiratory flow
A fall in FVC of 10% with preserved FEV₁
A 20% rise in FEV₁ after bronchodilator
investigations__LUNG FUNCTION__Provocati.answer: A 20% fall in FEV₁ from baseline
investigations__LUNG FUNCTION__Provocati.explanation: A positive bronchial provocation test is defined by a 20% fall in FEV₁ from baseline. The provocative dose or concentration producing this fall is reported as the PD20 or PC20.

investigations__LUNG FUNCTION__Provocati.question: Which statement best explains why bronchial provocation is most useful for excluding asthma?
options: It has very high negative predictive value, so a negative test largely rules out asthma
It is highly specific, so a positive test confirms asthma
It directly measures airway eosinophilia
It quantifies bronchodilator reversibility
It is diagnostic only when FEV₁ rises after methacholine
investigations__LUNG FUNCTION__Provocati.answer: It has very high negative predictive value, so a negative test largely rules out asthma
investigations__LUNG FUNCTION__Provocati.explanation: Airway hyper-responsiveness testing is sensitive with a high negative predictive value, meaning a negative result effectively excludes current asthma. It is less specific, as hyper-responsiveness also occurs in COPD and rhinitis.

investigations__LUNG FUNCTION__Provocati.question: In which patient is a methacholine challenge contraindicated?
options: A patient with mild allergic rhinitis and normal spirometry
A patient with a myocardial infarction two weeks ago
A patient with a resolved viral illness six weeks ago
A patient with a family history of asthma
A young adult with exercise-related cough
investigations__LUNG FUNCTION__Provocati.answer: A patient with a myocardial infarction two weeks ago
investigations__LUNG FUNCTION__Provocati.explanation: Recent myocardial infarction (within about three months) is a contraindication because induced bronchospasm and its cardiovascular stress can be dangerous. Other contraindications include severe airflow limitation, known aneurysm and uncontrolled hypertension.

investigations__LUNG FUNCTION__Provocati.question: A 22-year-old competitive swimmer reports cough and breathlessness only during hard training, with normal resting spirometry. Which test most specifically confirms exercise-induced bronchoconstriction and predicts steroid responsiveness?
options: Methacholine challenge
Inhaled mannitol challenge
Skin-prick allergen testing
Serum total IgE
Peak flow variability over one week
investigations__LUNG FUNCTION__Provocati.explanation: Mannitol is an indirect osmotic provocation test that triggers endogenous mediator release from inflamed airways, making it specific for asthma/EIB. A positive result reflects airway inflammation and predicts a good response to inhaled corticosteroids.

investigations__LUNG FUNCTION__Provocati.question: During a standardised exercise challenge, which fall in FEV₁ from baseline is the accepted threshold for a positive test for exercise-induced bronchoconstriction?
investigations__LUNG FUNCTION__Provocati.explanation: A ≥10% fall in FEV₁ after exercise defines a positive exercise challenge for EIB. Eucapnic voluntary hyperpnoea often uses a ≥15% cut-off to increase specificity.

investigations__LUNG FUNCTION__Provocati.question: Which statement best explains why indirect provocation tests are preferred over methacholine for confirming asthma in an athlete?
options: They act directly on smooth-muscle muscarinic receptors
They reflect airway inflammation and better predict inhaled-steroid response
They can be safely performed regardless of baseline FEV₁
They are more sensitive but far less specific than methacholine
They diagnose inducible laryngeal obstruction rather than asthma
investigations__LUNG FUNCTION__Provocati.answer: They reflect airway inflammation and better predict inhaled-steroid response
investigations__LUNG FUNCTION__Provocati.explanation: Indirect tests such as mannitol and exercise provoke endogenous mediator release from inflamed airways, so a positive result mirrors active inflammation. This specificity means the result predicts responsiveness to inhaled corticosteroids, guiding treatment.

investigations__LUNG FUNCTION__Provocati.question: According to NICE, what FeNO value is considered a positive result supporting asthma in an adult?
options: ≥ 15 ppb
≥ 25 ppb
≥ 40 ppb
≥ 60 ppb
≥ 100 ppb
investigations__LUNG FUNCTION__Provocati.explanation: NICE defines an adult FeNO of 40 ppb or greater as positive, adding weight to an asthma diagnosis. In children aged 5–16 the corresponding threshold is 35 ppb.

investigations__LUNG FUNCTION__Provocati.question: A 45-year-old with suspected asthma has a low FeNO. Which factor most likely explains a falsely low reading?
options: Coexisting allergic rhinitis
Current cigarette smoking
A nitrate-rich meal an hour earlier
Recent pollen exposure
Untreated atopic eczema
investigations__LUNG FUNCTION__Provocati.explanation: Smoking lowers exhaled nitric oxide and can mask genuine eosinophilic inflammation, producing a falsely reassuring result. Allergic rhinitis, atopy and nitrate-rich food tend to raise FeNO rather than lower it.

investigations__LUNG FUNCTION__Provocati.question: What is the underlying biochemical mechanism that causes FeNO to rise in eosinophilic airway inflammation?
options: Neutrophil elastase release breaking down elastin
IL-13-driven upregulation of inducible nitric oxide synthase (iNOS) in airway epithelium
Increased carbon monoxide production from haem breakdown
Mast cell histamine causing bronchial smooth muscle contraction
Reduced surfactant production by type II pneumocytes
investigations__LUNG FUNCTION__Provocati.answer: IL-13-driven upregulation of inducible nitric oxide synthase (iNOS) in airway epithelium
investigations__LUNG FUNCTION__Provocati.explanation: Type-2 cytokines such as IL-13 upregulate iNOS in bronchial epithelial cells, increasing nitric oxide that diffuses into the airway and is exhaled. This makes FeNO a marker of corticosteroid-responsive eosinophilic inflammation.

investigations__LUNG FUNCTION__Gas Trans.question: A 60-year-old smoker has airflow obstruction on spirometry. Which transfer factor pattern most strongly favours emphysema over asthma as the cause?
options: Reduced TLCO and reduced KCO
Raised TLCO with normal KCO
Normal TLCO with raised KCO
Reduced TLCO with markedly raised KCO
Normal TLCO and normal KCO
investigations__LUNG FUNCTION__Gas Trans.explanation: Emphysema destroys the alveolar-capillary surface area, so both the whole-lung transfer factor and the transfer coefficient per litre fall. Asthma characteristically preserves or raises TLCO, so a reduced TLCO and KCO discriminates emphysema from asthma.

investigations__LUNG FUNCTION__Gas Trans.question: A patient with restrictive spirometry has a low TLCO but a preserved (indeed high) KCO. Which cause does this pattern most suggest?
options: Chest-wall or neuromuscular (extraparenchymal) restriction
Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis
Emphysema
Pulmonary embolism
Alveolar haemorrhage
investigations__LUNG FUNCTION__Gas Trans.explanation: When the lung tissue is normal but under-inflated, total CO transfer falls yet transfer per litre of ventilated lung is preserved or elevated. A low TLCO with high KCO therefore points to an extraparenchymal cause such as chest-wall deformity or neuromuscular weakness rather than intrinsic lung disease.

investigations__LUNG FUNCTION__Gas Trans.question: A transfer factor report shows a reduced TLCO. Before attributing this to lung disease, which correction is essential?
options: Correction for the patient's haemoglobin
Correction for body surface area
Correction for arterial oxygen saturation
Correction for FEV1/FVC ratio
Correction for resting heart rate
investigations__LUNG FUNCTION__Gas Trans.explanation: CO uptake depends on the haemoglobin available in the pulmonary capillaries, so TLCO must be corrected for measured Hb. Uncorrected anaemia falsely lowers the value and can be mislabelled as fibrosis or pulmonary vascular disease.

investigations__LUNG FUNCTION__Gas Trans.question: A patient with severe bullous emphysema has lung volumes measured by both helium dilution and body plethysmography on the same day. How will the results compare?
options: Helium dilution will give a lower TLC than plethysmography
Helium dilution will give a higher TLC than plethysmography
Both methods will give identical values
Plethysmography will fail to detect the trapped gas
Helium dilution measures gas in the bullae more accurately
investigations__LUNG FUNCTION__Gas Trans.answer: Helium dilution will give a lower TLC than plethysmography
investigations__LUNG FUNCTION__Gas Trans.explanation: Helium only equilibrates into airspaces communicating with open airways, so the gas trapped inside bullae is not sampled and TLC is underestimated. Plethysmography measures all compressible intrathoracic gas via Boyle's law and reads higher, which is why it is the gold standard in bullous disease.

investigations__LUNG FUNCTION__Gas Trans.question: Which single measured value is required to confirm a restrictive ventilatory defect?
options: A reduced total lung capacity (TLC)
A reduced FEV1/FVC ratio
A reduced FEV1 alone
An increased residual volume (RV)
An increased RV/TLC ratio
investigations__LUNG FUNCTION__Gas Trans.explanation: Restriction is defined by a TLC below the lower limit of normal, reflecting a genuinely small lung. A reduced FEV1/FVC indicates obstruction, and raised RV or RV/TLC indicate gas trapping rather than restriction.

investigations__LUNG FUNCTION__Gas Trans.question: Body plethysmography derives thoracic gas volume by applying which physical principle?
options: Boyle's law relating pressure and volume of the trapped gas
Fick's principle of gas diffusion across the alveolar membrane
Henry's law of gas solubility in blood
Graham's law of gas diffusion rates
Dalton's law of partial pressures
investigations__LUNG FUNCTION__Gas Trans.answer: Boyle's law relating pressure and volume of the trapped gas
investigations__LUNG FUNCTION__Gas Trans.explanation: During panting against a closed shutter the trapped thoracic gas is compressed and expanded, and the reciprocal pressure and volume changes are solved using Boyle's law (P1V1 = P2V2). This yields the thoracic gas volume at FRC including non-communicating gas.

investigations__LUNG FUNCTION__Gas Trans.question: During body plethysmography, what does closing a shutter at the mouthpiece while the patient pants allow the system to determine?
options: The forced expiratory volume in one second
Alveolar pressure, since mouth pressure equilibrates with it during occlusion
The diffusing capacity for carbon monoxide
The maximal inspiratory mouth pressure of the respiratory muscles
The residual volume by nitrogen washout
investigations__LUNG FUNCTION__Gas Trans.answer: Alveolar pressure, since mouth pressure equilibrates with it during occlusion
investigations__LUNG FUNCTION__Gas Trans.explanation: When the shutter occludes the airway there is no flow, so mouth pressure equilibrates with alveolar pressure. Measuring this alongside airflow (with the shutter open) lets the box calculate airway resistance.

investigations__LUNG FUNCTION__Gas Trans.question: A child with poor spirometry coordination undergoes plethysmography showing raised Raw and low sGaw that improves markedly after salbutamol. What does this indicate?
options: A restrictive ventilatory defect
Reversible airflow obstruction consistent with asthma
A fixed large-airway stenosis
Normal airway function
Impaired alveolar gas diffusion
investigations__LUNG FUNCTION__Gas Trans.answer: Reversible airflow obstruction consistent with asthma
investigations__LUNG FUNCTION__Gas Trans.explanation: Raised Raw with low sGaw signifies airflow obstruction, and a marked rise in sGaw after a bronchodilator demonstrates reversibility. This effort-independent pattern strongly supports asthma, especially valuable when spirometry is unreliable.

investigations__LUNG FUNCTION__Gas Trans.question: Why is specific airway conductance (sGaw) preferred over raw airway resistance (Raw) alone when comparing measurements?
options: It measures only the small peripheral airways
It is normalised to lung volume, since resistance varies with the volume at which it is measured
It requires a forced maximal expiratory effort
It reflects alveolar-capillary gas transfer
It is unaffected by bronchodilator therapy
investigations__LUNG FUNCTION__Gas Trans.answer: It is normalised to lung volume, since resistance varies with the volume at which it is measured
investigations__LUNG FUNCTION__Gas Trans.explanation: Airway resistance falls as lung volume rises because airways are tethered open, so Raw is uninterpretable without its volume. Dividing conductance by lung volume gives sGaw, a volume-corrected index allowing valid comparison between patients and over time.

investigations__LUNG FUNCTION__Gas Trans.question: The Lung Clearance Index is calculated from a multiple-breath washout as the cumulative expired volume divided by which parameter?
options: Forced vital capacity (FVC)
Functional residual capacity (FRC)
Total lung capacity (TLC)
Peak expiratory flow rate (PEFR)
Residual volume (RV)
investigations__LUNG FUNCTION__Gas Trans.explanation: LCI equals cumulative expired volume divided by FRC, representing the number of lung turnovers needed to clear the tracer. FRC is itself derived from the dilution of the inert tracer gas during the washout.

investigations__LUNG FUNCTION__Gas Trans.question: In multiple-breath washout, the test endpoint is reached when the end-tidal tracer gas concentration falls to what fraction of its starting value?
investigations__LUNG FUNCTION__Gas Trans.explanation: Washout continues until the tracer concentration reaches 1/40th (2.5%) of its initial value. The cumulative expired volume needed to reach this point is the numerator of the LCI calculation.

investigations__LUNG FUNCTION__Gas Trans.question: Which statement best explains why LCI is favoured over spirometry for detecting early lung disease in cystic fibrosis?
options: It requires a maximal forced expiratory effort
It becomes abnormal only after FEV1 has already fallen
It is more sensitive and detects small-airways disease earlier, while being feasible during tidal breathing
It specifically identifies the causative organism of infection
It measures large-airway obstruction more accurately than FEV1
investigations__LUNG FUNCTION__Gas Trans.answer: It is more sensitive and detects small-airways disease earlier, while being feasible during tidal breathing
investigations__LUNG FUNCTION__Gas Trans.explanation: LCI detects peripheral ventilation inhomogeneity and can be abnormal when spirometry is still normal, marking it the earliest sign of CF lung disease. Because it uses effort-independent tidal breathing it is also achievable in young children.
